¶
'''3.''' To do like work at a less price than: as, one mason may ''underwork'' another.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To work in secret or clandestinely. ''B. Jonson.''—'''2.''' To do less work than is required or suitable.

'''underworker''' (un′dėr-wėr″kėr), ''n.'' [< ''underwork'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who underworks.—'''2.''' A subordinate workman; one who works in subjection to another. ''Swift'', Nobles and Commons, iv.

'''under-workman''' (un′dėr-wėrk″ma̤n), ''n.''; pl. ''underworkmen'' (-men). An inferior or subordinate workman. ''Swift.''

'''under-world''' (un′dėr-wėrld), ''n.'' '''1.''' The world below the skies; this lower world; the sublunary world.
{{smaller block|<poem>Loud Fame calls ye,
Pitch’d on the topless Apennine, and blows
To all the ''under-world'', all nations, the seas,
And unfrequented deserts where the snow dwells.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Bonduca, iii. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' The opposite side of the globe; the antipodes.
{{smaller block|<poem>Fresh as the first beam glittering on a sail
That brings our friends up from the ''under-world''.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', The Princess (song).}}}}
'''3.''' The world below this world; the infernal world; the place or state of departed souls; Hades.
{{smaller block|Hades. The ghosts of Homer live in the ''underworld'', depleted of all that fresh and throbbing life which they had on the earth.
{{right|''E. H. Sears'', The Fourth Gospel, the Heart of Christ.}}}}
'''4.''' The lower, inferior, degraded part of man-

{{smaller block|His humorous predominance.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 3. 137}}}}

¶
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To practise insuring, particularly marine insuring; carry on the busines of an underwriter. ''F. Martin'', Hist. of Lloyd’s p. 365.

'''underwriter''' (un′dėr-rī″tėr), ''n.'' One who insures, or carries on a business of insurance especially of marine insurance.—{{smaller|'''Underwriters wire''', wire the use of which for electrical purposes is authorized by the underwriters for fire-insurance.}}

'''underwriting''' (un′dėr-rī″ting), ''n.'' [Verbal n of ''underwrite'', ''v.''] The practice or business o an underwriter. See ''underwriter''.

'''underyoke†''' (un-dėr-yōk′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''under yoken''; < ''under'' + ''yoke''.] To bring under th yoke; make subject.
{{smaller block|Al the erthe he shulde ''vnduryoke'' to his empire.
{{right|''Wyclif'', Judith ii.}}}}

'''undescendible, undescendable''' (un-dẹ̄-sen′di-bl, -da-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not descendible; hence, unfathomable. ''Tennyson'', Harold, i. 1.—'''2.''' No capable of descending to heirs.

'''undescribable''' (un-des-krī′ba-bl), ''a.'' Indescribable. ''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv. 53. [Rare.

'''undescribed''' (un-des-krībd′), ''a.'' Not describe not depicted, defined, or delineated: as, an ''undescribed'' species.

'''undescried''' (un-des-krīd′), ''a.'' Not descried; n discovered; not seen.

'''undeserve''' (un-dẹ̄-zėrv′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''deserve''.] To fail to deserve. [Rare.]
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''undeservedly''' (un-dē-zėr′ved-li), ''adv.'' Without desert, either good or evil; contrary to desert or what is merited.
{{smaller block|Athletick brutes whom ''undeservedly'' we call heroes.
{{right|''Dryden'', Pal. and Arc., Ded.}}}}

'''undeservedness''' (un-dẹ̄-zėr′ved-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being undeserved.

'''undeserver''' (un-dē-zėr′vėr), ''n.'' One of no merit; one who is not deserving or worthy.
{{smaller block|<poem>To sell and mart your offices for gold
To ''undeservers''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., iv. 3. 12.}}}}

'''undeserving''' (un-dē-zėr′ving), ''p. a.'' '''1.''' Not deserving; not having merit.
{{smaller block|<poem>Your gracious favours
Done to me, ''undeserving'' as I am.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1. 7.}}}}
'''2.''' Not meriting: with ''of'': as, a man ''undeserving of'' happiness or ''of'' punishment.
{{smaller block|''Undeserving of'' destruction.{{right|''Sir P. Sidney.''}}}}

'''undeservingly''' (un-dē-zėr′ving-li), ''adv.'' Without meriting; undeservedly. ''Milton.''

'''undesigned''' (un-dē-zīnd′), ''a.'' Not designed; not intended; unintentional; not proceeding from purpose: as, to do an ''undesigned'' injury. ''Paley'', Evidences, iii. 6.

'''undesignedly''' (un-dē-zī′ned-li), ''adv.'' In an undesigned manner; without design or intention. ''Paley'', Evidences, i. 3.

'''undesignedness''' (un-dē-zī′ned-nes), ''n.'' The state or character of being undesigned; freedom from design or set purpose. ''Paley'', Evidences, iii. 7.
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''undesigning''' (un-dē-zī′ning), ''a.'' Not having any underhand design; sincere; upright; artless; having no artful or fraudulent purpose.
{{smaller block|Weak, ''undesigning'' minds. {{right|''South'', Sermons.}}}}

'''undesirability''' (un-dẹ̄-zīr-a̤-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' The condition or character of being undesirable.

'''undesirable''' (un-dẹ̄-zīr′a̤-bl), ''a.'' Not desirable; not to be wished.
{{smaller block|A thing not ''undesirable.'' {{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 823.}}}}

'''undesirableness''' (un-dẹ̄-zīr′a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character or state of being undesirable; undesirability.

'''undesirably''' (un-dẹ̄-zīr′a̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an undesirable manner; contrary to what is desirable.

'''undesired''' (un-dẹ̄-zīrd′), ''a.'' Not desired; not solicited. ''Dryden.''

'''undesiring''' (un-dẹ̄-zīr′ing), ''a.'' Not desiring; not wishing. ''Dryden'', tr. of Persius, satire 5.

'''undesirous''' (un-dẹ̄-zīr′us), ''a.'' Not desirous.

'''undespairing''' (un-des-pãr′ing), ''a.'' Not yielding to despair. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|With steady ''undespairing'' breast. {{right|''Dyer'', The Fleece, iv.}}}}

'''undespiteous†''' (un-des-pit′ẹ̄-us), ''a.'' Lacking in despite; piteous; kind.
{{smaller block|<poem>Save onely a looke piteous
Of womanhead ''undispiteous.''</poem>
{{right|''The Isle of Ladies'', l. 676.}}}}

'''undespondent''' (un-des-pon′de̤nt), ''a.'' Not marked by or given to despondency.
{{smaller block|Sorrowing but ''undespondent'' years.
{{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 2d ser., p. 119.}}}}
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''undestined''' (un-des′tind), ''a.'' Not destined ''R. Pollok.''

'''undestroyable†''' (un-des-troi′a-bl), ''a.'' Indestructible. ''Boyle'', Works, III. 283.

'''undeterminable''' (un-dẹ̄-tėr′mi-na̤-bl), ''a.'' Indeterminable. ''Locke'', Human Understanding, ii 17.

'''undeterminate''' (un-dẹ̄-tėr′mi-nạ̄t), ''a.'' Indeterminate. ''South.''

'''undeterminateness''' (un-dē-tėr′mi-nāt-nes), ''n'' Indeterminateness. ''Dr. H. More'', Divine Dialogues.

'''undetermination''' (un-dē-tėr-mi-nā′sho̤n), ''n'' Indetermination. ''Sir M. Hale'', Orig. of Mankind, p. 61.

'''undetermined''' (un-dẹ̄-tėr′mind), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not determined; not settled; not decided.
{{smaller block|''Undetermined'' differences of kings.
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 35}}}}
'''2.''' Indeterminate.
{{smaller block|Wit seems to be one of these ''undetermined'' sounds which we affix scarce any precise idea.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', The Bee, No.}}}}

'''undetesting''' (un-dē-tes′ting), ''a.'' Not detesting not abhorring. ''Thomson'', Liberty, v. 293.

'''undeviating''' (un-dē′vi-ā-ting), ''a.'' Not deviating; not departing from a rule, principle, or purpose; uniform; regular.
{{smaller block|Heaven, we are assured, is much more pleased to view a repentant sinner than ninety-nine persons who have supported a course of ''undeviating'' rectitude.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Vicar, xx}}}}
readings.c3s1:
¶
'''undeviatingly''' (un-dē′vi-ā-ting-li), ''adv.'' Without deviation; steadily.

'''undevil†''' (un-dev′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''devil.''] To free from possession by the devil; exorcise. ''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., X. iv. 54.

'''undevised''' (un-dē-vīzd′), ''a.'' Not devised; not bequeathed by will. ''Blackstone.''

'''undevoted''' (un-dē-vō′ted), ''a.'' Not devoted. ''Clarendon'', Civil War, I. 117.

'''undevotion''' (un-dē-vō′shọn), ''n.'' [< ME. ''undevocioun''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''devotion.''] Lack of devotion or devoutness. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Thanne comth ''undevocioun'', thurgh which a man . . . hath swich languor in soule that he may neither rede ne singe in holy chirche, ne heere ne thynke of no devocioun.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}}}

'''undevout''' (un-dẹ̄-vout′), ''a.'' Not devout; having no devotion.
{{smaller block|An ''undevout'' astronomer is mad.
{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, ix.}}}}

'''undevoutly''' (un-dẹ̄-vout′li), ''adv.'' In an undevout manner; without devotion.

'''undiademed''' (un-dī′a̤-demd), ''a.'' Not having or wearing a diadem or crown; uncrowned.

'''undiaphanous''' (un-dī-af′a-nus), ''a.'' Not diaphanous. ''Boyle'', Works, III. 57.

'''undifferencing''' (un-dif′e̤-ren-sing), ''a.'' Not marking any difference; impartial. ''Chapman.'' [Rare.]

'''undifferent†''' (un-dif′e-rent), ''a.'' [< ME. ''undifferent''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''different.''] Not different.
{{smaller block|<poem>The fourme of tho freikes was, faithfully to se,
Right suche as the syre, that I said first;
''Vndifferent'' to deme fro there dere fader.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3915.}}}}
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''undifferentiated''' (un-dif-e-ren′shi-ā-ted), ''a.'' Not differentiated; without clear distinctive characters: often used by naturalists to note species or groups which do not show well-marked distinctive characters, or, according to the theory of evolution, are not yet completely separated from other species or groups.

'''undigenous''' (un-dij′e-nus), ''a.'' [< L. ''unda'' (√ ''ud-'', ''und-''), wave, + ''gignere'', *''genera'' (√ ''gen-''), produce, + ''-ous''.] Generated by, or owing origin to, water. ''Kirwan.'' [Rare.]

'''undigested''' (un-di-jes′ted), ''a.'' Not digested, in any sense.
{{smaller block|Filled with fumes of ''undigested'' wine.
{{right|''Selden'', note to Drayton’s Polyolbion, xvii.}}}}

'''undigestible''' (un-di-jes′ti-bl), ''a.'' Indigestible.

'''undight†''' (un-dīt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''dight''.] To put off, as ornaments or apparel.
{{smaller block|From her fayre head her fillet she ''undight.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. iii. 4.}}}}

'''undigne†''', ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''digne''.] Unworthy.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Undigne'' and unworthy
Am I to thilke honour that ye me bede.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Clerk’s Tale, l. 303.}}}}

'''undignified''' (un-dig′ni-fīd), ''a.'' Not dignified. {{smaller|(''a'') Not honored; not rendered dignified. (''b'') Not consistent with dignity; exhibiting an absence of dignity.}}
{{smaller block|The attempts of Henry III. to influence the chapters were ''undignified'' and unsuccessful; his candidates were seldom chosen. {{right|''Stubbs'', Const. Hist., § 705.}}}}

'''undignify''' (un-dig′ni-fī), ''v. t.'' To render undignified; deprive of dignity; debase. [Rare.] ''Howells'', Venetian Life, xii.

'''undilution''' (un-di-lū′shọn), ''n.'' The character or state of being undiluted. [Rare.]
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|The three primary colours assumed in the . . . figure (of the prismatic spectrum) are red, green, and blue, each in its highest degree of purity and ''undilution''.
{{right|''Herschel'', Popular Lectures on Scientific Subjects, p. 258.}}}}

'''undinal''' (un-dē′nal), ''a.'' [< ''undine'' + ''-al''.] Of or pertaining to an undine, or the belief in such creatures.

'''undine''' (un-dēn′), ''n.'' [= F. ''ondine'', f. (''ondin'', m.), = G. ''undine'', < NL. *''undina'', a water-spirit, < L. ''unda'', wave, water: see ''undulate'', ''ound''.] A water-spirit of the female sex, resembling in character the sylphs or spirits of the air, and corresponding in some measure to the naiads of classical mythology. According to Paracelsus, when an undine married a mortal and bore a child she received a soul.

'''undinted''' (un-din′ted), ''a.'' Not impressed by blows; unbattered. ''Shak.'', A. and C., ii. 6. 39.

'''undiocesed''' (un-dī′ọ̄-sēst), ''a.'' Not possessed of or preferred to a diocese. ''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.

'''undirect†''' (un-di-rekt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''direct''.] To misdirect; mislead. ''Fuller.''

'''undirectly''' (un-di-rekt′li), ''adv.'' Indirectly. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Directly or ''undirectly'', secretly or openly.
{{right|''Strype'', Eccles. Mem., Henry VIII. No. 64.}}}}

'''undiscernable''' (un-di-zėr′na̤-bl), ''a.'' Same as ''undiscernible''.

'''undevised''' (un-dē-vīzd′), ''a.'' Not devised; not bequeathed by will. ''Blackstone.''

'''undevoted''' (un-dē-vō′ted), ''a.'' Not devoted. ''Clarendon'', Civil War, I. 117.

'''undevotion''' (un-dē-vō′shọn), ''n.'' [< ME. ''undevocioun''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''devotion.''] Lack of devotion or devoutness. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Thanne comth ''undevocioun'', thurgh which a man . . . hath swich languor in soule that he may neither rede ne singe in holy chirche, ne heere ne thynke of no devocioun.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parson’s Tale.}}}}

'''undevout''' (un-dẹ̄-vout′), ''a.'' Not devout; having no devotion.
{{smaller block|An ''undevout'' astronomer is mad.
{{right|''Young'', Night Thoughts, ix.}}}}

'''undevoutly''' (un-dẹ̄-vout′li), ''adv.'' In an undevout manner; without devotion.

'''undiademed''' (un-dī′a̤-demd), ''a.'' Not having or wearing a diadem or crown; uncrowned.

'''undiaphanous''' (un-dī-af′a-nus), ''a.'' Not diaphanous. ''Boyle'', Works, III. 57.

'''undifferencing''' (un-dif′e̤-ren-sing), ''a.'' Not marking any difference; impartial. ''Chapman.'' [Rare.]

'''undifferent†''' (un-dif′e-rent), ''a.'' [< ME. ''undifferent''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''different.''] Not different.
{{smaller block|<poem>The fourme of tho freikes was, faithfully to se,
Right suche as the syre, that I said first;
''Vndifferent'' to deme fro there dere fader.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3915.}}}}

'''undifferentiated''' (un-dif-e-ren′shi-ā-ted), ''a.'' Not differentiated; without clear distinctive characters: often used by naturalists to note species or groups which do not show well-marked distinctive characters, or, according to the theory of evolution, are not yet completely separated from other species or groups.

'''undigenous''' (un-dij′e-nus), ''a.'' [< L. ''unda'' (√ ''ud-'', ''und-''), wave, + ''gignere'', *''genera'' (√ ''gen-''), produce, + ''-ous''.] Generated by, or owing origin to, water. ''Kirwan.'' [Rare.]

'''undigested''' (un-di-jes′ted), ''a.'' Not digested, in any sense.
{{smaller block|Filled with fumes of ''undigested'' wine.
{{right|''Selden'', note to Drayton’s Polyolbion, xvii.}}}}

'''undigestible''' (un-di-jes′ti-bl), ''a.'' Indigestible.

'''undight†''' (un-dīt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''dight''.] To put off, as ornaments or apparel.
{{smaller block|From her fayre head her fillet she ''undight.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. iii. 4.}}}}

'''undigne†''', ''a.'' [ME., < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''digne''.] Unworthy.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Undigne'' and unworthy
Am I to thilke honour that ye me bede.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Clerk’s Tale, l. 303.}}}}

'''undignified''' (un-dig′ni-fīd), ''a.'' Not dignified. {{smaller|(''a'') Not honored; not rendered dignified. (''b'') Not consistent with dignity; exhibiting an absence of dignity.}}
{{smaller block|The attempts of Henry III. to influence the chapters were ''undignified'' and unsuccessful; his candidates were seldom chosen. {{right|''Stubbs'', Const. Hist., § 705.}}}}

'''undignify''' (un-dig′ni-fī), ''v. t.'' To render undignified; deprive of dignity; debase. [Rare.] ''Howells'', Venetian Life, xii.

'''undilution''' (un-di-lū′shọn), ''n.'' The character or state of being undiluted. [Rare.] {{smaller block|The three primary colours assumed in the . . . figure (of the prismatic spectrum) are red, green, and blue, each in its highest degree of purity and ''undilution''.
{{right|''Herschel'', Popular Lectures on Scientific Subjects, p. 258.}}}}

'''undinal''' (un-dē′nal), ''a.'' [< ''undine'' + ''-al''.] Of or pertaining to an undine, or the belief in such creatures.

'''undine''' (un-dēn′), ''n.'' [= F. ''ondine'', f. (''ondin'', m.), = G. ''undine'', < NL. *''undina'', a water-spirit, < L. ''unda'', wave, water: see ''undulate'', ''ound''.] A water-spirit of the female sex, resembling in character the sylphs or spirits of the air, and corresponding in some measure to the naiads of classical mythology. According to Paracelsus, when an undine married a mortal and bore a child she received a soul.

'''undinted''' (un-din′ted), ''a.'' Not impressed by blows; unbattered. ''Shak.'', A. and C., ii. 6. 39.

'''undiocesed''' (un-dī′ọ̄-sēst), ''a.'' Not possessed of or preferred to a diocese. ''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., i.

'''undirect†''' (un-di-rekt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''direct''.] To misdirect; mislead. ''Fuller.''

'''undirectly''' (un-di-rekt′li), ''adv.'' Indirectly. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Directly or ''undirectly'', secretly or openly.
{{right|''Strype'', Eccles. Mem., Henry VIII. No. 64.}}}}

'''undiscernable''' (un-di-zėr′na̤-bl), ''a.'' Same as ''undiscernible''.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
